LanguageData.HR_Event_WesternZhouCrisis_771BCE_Descri: King You died during the crisis that ended Western Zhou rule at the western capital. This entry records broad traditional chronology without replaying the event.
LanguageData.HR_Event_WesternZhouCrisis_771BCE_Source: Sima Qian, Shiji, vol. 4, “Zhou Benji”; CText text node 4615. The BCE year follows conventional chronology.
LanguageData.HR_Event_ZhouEasternMigration_770BCE_Des: King Ping moved the Zhou court east to Luoyi, the conventional beginning of the Eastern Zhou period.
LanguageData.HR_Event_ZhouEasternMigration_770BCE_Sou: Sima Qian, Shiji, vol. 4, “Zhou Benji”; CText parallel passage node 4658. The BCE year follows conventional chronology.

LanguageData.HR_Event_QinXiangRecognition_770BCE_Desc: Traditional accounts say Lord Xiang of Qin aided King Ping's eastward move and received recognition as a regional lord. This does not establish that Qin had conquered all western lands.
LanguageData.HR_Event_QinXiangRecognition_770BCE_Sour: Shiji, Qin Benji; compare Pengcheng Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), section “The Chronology of Qin”. The event is a chronicle entry only.
LanguageData.HR_Event_XieKingDeath_750BCE_Label: Death of King Hui of Xie (disputed date)
LanguageData.HR_Event_XieKingDeath_750BCE_Description: A traditional reconstruction places the rival Zhou ruler's death around 750 BCE. The chronology is contested; this chronicle-only entry does not resolve the succession dispute in the world state.
LanguageData.HR_Event_XieKingDeath_750BCE_SourceNotes: Chen Minzhen and Yuri Pines, “Where is King Ping? The History and Historiography of the Zhou Dynasty’s Eastward Relocation” (2018); Pengcheng Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), pp. 589–614, proposes a different Xie chronology (779–759 BCE). The date is deliberately year-only and disputed. https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/where-is-king-ping-the-history-and-historiography-of-the-zhou-dyn/ ; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/early-china/article/chronology-of-western-zhou/0D661C3365537C0D15AD896F72F9DF70
LanguageData.HR_Event_JinQuwoEnfeoffment_745BCE_Label: Jin grants Quwo to a collateral branch
LanguageData.HR_Event_JinQuwoEnfeoffment_745BCE_Descr: Jin's Marquis Zhao establishes Chengshi at Quwo, beginning a long-running internal succession conflict. This entry records the chronicle event without simulating a conquest.
LanguageData.HR_Event_JinQuwoEnfeoffment_745BCE_Sourc: Zuo zhuan, Lord Hui 24 (traditional conversion 745 BCE); Edward L. Shaughnessy, A Brief History of Ancient China (2023), pp. 179–180. Year-only precision. https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9780295806730_A30891990/preview-9780295806730_A30891990.pdf
LanguageData.HR_Context_ZhengEasternExpansion_Descrip: Long-term political growth toward the eastern plains. Generated local incidents are fictional and do not claim specific conquests.
LanguageData.HR_Context_ZhengEasternExpansion_Sources: Shiji, Zheng Shijia; Pengcheng Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), section “The Chronology of Zheng.” Background range only; no single event date is asserted.
LanguageData.HR_Context_ZhengAndKuai_Description: Later accounts associate Zheng's growth with the Guo and Kuai polities, but accounts and chronologies conflict. This is a context for fictional local disputes, not a dated conquest.
LanguageData.HR_Context_ZhengAndKuai_Sources: Shiji, Zheng Shijia; Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), notes 135–136 and the Zheng chronology discussion. Competing accounts are retained.
LanguageData.HR_Context_RoyalCourtAtLuoyi_Description: Luoyi is the Zhou court's eastern center in the received narrative. The court's presence may frame fictional messengers and demands; those incidents are not attested.
LanguageData.HR_Context_RoyalCourtAtLuoyi_Sources: Shiji, Zhou Benji; Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), section “King Ping and King Hui of Xie.”
LanguageData.HR_Context_CompetingZhouLegitimacy_Descr: Accounts of King Ping and King Hui of Xie describe a contested transition after King You's death. Local reports should remain uncertain and must not reveal future outcomes.
LanguageData.HR_Context_CompetingZhouLegitimacy_Sourc: Qinghua University, Xinian, chapter 2; Chen Minzhen and Yuri Pines, “Where is King Ping?” Asia Major 31 (2018); Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou” (2023). Dates and sequence are contested.
LanguageData.HR_Context_JinSupportForPing_Description: Jin's Marquis Wen appears as an important supporter of King Ping in the Xinian account. This context does not create an unrecorded battle or territorial transfer.
LanguageData.HR_Context_JinSupportForPing_Sources: Xinian, chapter 2; Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), pp. 589–614.
LanguageData.HR_Context_QinWesternDevelopment_Descrip: Qin consolidates in the western region over time. The scenario does not treat the entire west as already conquered in 770 BCE.
LanguageData.HR_Context_QinWesternDevelopment_Sources: Shiji, Qin Benji; Zhang, “The Chronology of Western Zhou,” Early China 46 (2023), section “The Chronology of Qin.”
LanguageData.HR_Context_BronzeRitualObjects_Descripti: Bronze vessels and their inscriptions provide material and documentary context for elite ritual, political grants, and lineage identity.
LanguageData.HR_Context_BronzeRitualObjects_Sources: Edward L. Shaughnessy, “Western Zhou Archaeology,” Cambridge History of Ancient China; “Sources of Western Zhou History: Inscribed Bronze Vessels,” Society for the Study of Early China. Continuing material context, not a dated occurrence.
LanguageData.HR_Context_AncestralRituals_Description: Lineage rites and funerary practices are represented as social context; no particular village rite is asserted as historical fact.
LanguageData.HR_Context_AncestralRituals_Sources: “Bronze Vessels: Style, Assemblages, and Innovations of the Western Zhou Period,” Oxford Handbook of Early China; Shaughnessy, “Western Zhou Archaeology,” Cambridge History of Ancient China.
LanguageData.HR_Context_AgricultureAndStorage_Descrip: Farming, pottery, settlement life, and storage are recurring material conditions. The game uses them as scenario context without inventing a single-year invention.
LanguageData.HR_Context_AgricultureAndStorage_Sources: Xinyu Ren, Huangtucheng Regional Archaeological Survey (2008), pottery assemblage discussion; archaeological evidence is used as context rather than a dated historical event.
LanguageData.HR_Context_CraftTransmission_Description: Bronze casting, pottery, woodworking, and textile skills spread through craftspeople, materials, and regional exchange. This continuing context does not imply iron was common everywhere or date a specific invention.
LanguageData.HR_Context_CraftTransmission_Sources: Shiji, Qin Shijia and archaeological studies of Zhou-period craft production and exchange; context only, with no single event date asserted.
LanguageData.HR_RelicDef_BronzeVessel_Description: A gameplay-generated family heirloom. It is not a copy of a named archaeological object.
LanguageData.HR_Relic_BronzeVessel_Description: A bronze vessel created in the scenario as a fictional family heirloom.
